title: Exile in Burma
hook: Baba Ram Singh was exiled to Rangoon

segments.voice: Yesterday, Malerkotla, and your line was remembered. Whose name did you say? Today, what happened to the teacher himself. Day nine hundred sixty.

A ship pulls away from the coast of India, heading east across the Bay of Bengal. On board, under guard, is a man in white who has never been tried for any crime. He's being taken to Rangoon, in Burma, a country where he doesn't speak the language, far from his village, his people and the fields of the Punjab. The British have decided to keep Baba Ram Singh far from anyone who might gather around him. Today: exile in Burma.
screen: `A SHIP HEADING EAST.` → `A MAN IN WHITE, UNDER GUARD.` → `NEVER TRIED.` → `RANGOON, FAR FROM THE PUNJAB.`

segments.voice: First, the arrest. After Malerkotla, the British took Baba Ram Singh into custody, even though, as you heard yesterday, Namdhari histories say he hadn't sent the raiders. He wasn't put on trial. Instead, the government used an old regulation that let it hold a person as a state prisoner without charges, and sent him far from the Punjab, across the sea. Second, the place. Burma was then ruled from British India, and Rangoon was its port city. For a teacher whose whole life was a village, a congregation and the sound of the Name recited together, this was very far from home. He was kept under watch, with few of his own people allowed near. Third, the letters. Namdharis keep letters said to have been written by Baba Ram Singh in exile and carried back to the Punjab. In them, the community remembers, he encouraged his followers to hold to the Name and to their discipline. Exile cut the road, but not every thread. Fourth, how the story ends, and who says what. British records say he died in Burma. Namdhari tradition holds that he did not die there, and looks for his return. That belief belongs to the Namdhari community, and this lesson simply reports it. Punjabi has a word for the one far from home: pardesi, the traveler in a strange land. Some readers of the Guru's hymns hear the soul itself pictured that way, a guest in this world, longing for home. Baba Ram Singh lived that picture in his body.
screen: `HELD WITHOUT TRIAL.` · `RANGOON, A PORT FAR EAST.` · `LETTERS CARRIED HOME.` · `WHO SAYS WHAT ABOUT THE END.` · then, large: `FAR FROM HOME.`

segments.voice: Two minutes for the exiled. Sit, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind someone who lives far from home, not by choice: a refugee, a prisoner, a person sent away, someone who can't go back. You don't need to know their name. Picture them waking up somewhere strange today. On each breath out, wish them one thing: safety, or a letter from home, or a familiar voice. If you pray, you can hold them before Waheguru in the quiet. The bell holds the time.
Pardesi, the one far from home, a traveler in a strange land: Baba Ram Singh, held without trial, sent to Rangoon, remembered by his followers through his letters. Today's word.
Your line: far from home. Today, if someone near you comes from far away, ask them one thing about home, and listen to the answer. Day nine hundred sixty.

howItsDone: Namdhari Sikhs remember Baba Ram Singh's exile to Burma, keep letters they hold he wrote from there, and Namdhari tradition looks for his return.

Editor: cut the superlative 'about as far as the empire could send him'; recast the unsourced 'Sikh writing has an old word' and Gurbani claim as Punjabi usage and 'some readers'; changed the carry action, which repeated day 949's message to someone far from home.

Auditor: fixed a factual error, 'sent him out of India altogether', which contradicted the next line: Burma was then governed as part of British India. Softened the hook's 'somewhere nobody can reach him' (followers did send and receive letters, as the teach says).
